# Judith Chapter 13 — Disagreement Log

**Date:** 2026-03-17
**Chapter:** Judith 13 (20 verses)
**Theme:** THE CLIMAX — Judith beheads Holofernes; return to Bethulia; reception and praise

---

## Disagreement Count: 22

---

### Disagreement 1 — Verse 1: Servants' departure

**EMET:** "his servants quickly withdrew"
**LOGOS:** "his servants withdrew in haste"
**PNEUMA:** "his servants cleared out quickly"

**Issue:** Greek exanestēsan — they rose up and left. The adverb tachos/tachu implied. "Quickly" vs. "in haste" vs. "cleared out."
**SOPHIA ruling:** "His servants withdrew in haste" — more formal; "cleared out" is too colloquial for the register.

---

### Disagreement 2 — Verse 2: Holofernes' state

**EMET:** "overcome with wine"
**LOGOS:** "drowned in wine"
**PNEUMA:** "drowned in wine"

**Issue:** Greek pephyrmenon oinō — saturated/soaked/drowned in wine. LOGOS and PNEUMA independently render "drowned in wine," which is closer to the Greek image of total saturation.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "Drowned in wine" adopted. More accurate and vivid.

---

### Disagreement 3 — Verse 3: Judith's arrangement with her servant

**EMET:** "she told her servant to stand outside the bedchamber and to wait for her to come out, just as she did every day"
**LOGOS:** "She had told her servant to stand outside the bedchamber and wait for her to come out, as she did every day"
**PNEUMA:** "She had already told her servant to wait outside the bedchamber and watch for her"

**Issue:** PNEUMA adds "already" (not in text) and changes "stand" to "wait and watch." Minor.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "She had told her servant to stand outside the bedchamber and wait for her to come out, as she did every day."

---

### Disagreement 4 — Verse 4: Judith's prayer — "power" vs. "might" vs. "strength"

**EMET:** "O LORD God of all power"
**LOGOS:** "O LORD God of all power"
**PNEUMA:** "O LORD God of all power"

**Issue:** Unanimous — no disagreement. Greek pantokratōr kyrie theos.
**Note:** All three agree — logged for completeness.

---

### Disagreement 5 — Verse 4: "exaltation of Jerusalem" vs. "uplifting of Jerusalem"

**EMET:** "for the exaltation of Jerusalem"
**LOGOS:** "for the exaltation of Jerusalem"
**PNEUMA:** "for the exaltation of Jerusalem"

**Issue:** Unanimous on "exaltation." Logged for completeness.

---

### Disagreement 6 — Verse 5: "accomplish my purpose" vs. "accomplish my design"

**EMET:** "accomplish my purpose"
**LOGOS:** "accomplish my design"
**PNEUMA:** "accomplish what I have come for"

**Issue:** Greek epitelesai — to bring to completion. "Purpose," "design," and "what I have come for" all render this. PNEUMA paraphrases.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "Accomplish my purpose" — direct and fits the register of the prayer.

---

### Disagreement 7 — Verse 6: Judith approaching the bedpost

**EMET:** "She went to the bedpost that was by Holofernes' head"
**LOGOS:** "She went to the bedpost at Holofernes' head"
**PNEUMA:** "She crossed the tent to the bedpost at Holofernes' head"

**Issue:** PNEUMA adds "crossed the tent" — a logical inference about movement but not in the text.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "She went to the bedpost at Holofernes' head" — literal and sufficient.

---

### Disagreement 8 — Verse 7: The prayer before the act

**EMET:** "Strengthen me, O LORD God of Israel, this day"
**LOGOS:** "Give me strength, O LORD God of Israel, this day"
**PNEUMA:** "Give me strength, O LORD God of Israel, this day"

**Issue:** "Strengthen me" vs. "Give me strength" — both render krataioson me. Minor phrasing difference.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "Give me strength, O LORD God of Israel, this day" — slightly more natural in English prayer register.

---

### Disagreement 9 — Verse 8: THE CENTRAL SENTENCE

**EMET:** "She struck his neck twice with all her strength, and cut off his head from him."
**LOGOS:** "She struck his neck twice with all her might and cut off his head."
**PNEUMA:** "She struck his neck with all her might — once, twice — and cut off his head."

**Issue:** Three valid approaches:
- "Strength" vs. "might" — both render ischys
- "From him" in EMET is literal but slightly awkward
- PNEUMA's "once, twice" restructures the word order for dramatic effect

**SOPHIA ruling:** "She struck his neck twice with all her might and cut off his head." Clean, accurate, weighty. "Might" over "strength" for better sound with "twice." The numeral "twice" is not moved; it belongs where it is in the sentence.

---

### Disagreement 10 — Verse 9: Handling the body

**EMET:** "she rolled his body off the bed"
**LOGOS:** "She rolled his body from the bed"
**PNEUMA:** "She rolled his body from the bed"

**Issue:** "Off" vs. "from" — trivial. LOGOS/PNEUMA agree; EMET slightly more colloquial.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "She rolled his body from the bed."

---

### Disagreement 11 — Verse 9: "pulled down the canopy" vs. "took down the canopy"

**EMET:** "took down the canopy from the posts"
**LOGOS:** "pulled down the canopy from the posts"
**PNEUMA:** "pulled down the canopy from its posts"

**Issue:** "Took down" vs. "pulled down." The Greek katheileto — to take down from. Either works.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "Pulled down the canopy from the posts" — physical action word is more precise.

---

### Disagreement 12 — Verse 10: "food bag" vs. "food sack"

**EMET:** "her food bag"
**LOGOS:** "her food bag"
**PNEUMA:** "the food bag"

**Issue:** All use "food bag." Minor article variation in PNEUMA.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "Her food bag" — the possessive establishes it as the same bag introduced earlier.

---

### Disagreement 13 — Verse 10: Journey description

**EMET:** "they went around that valley and went up the mountain"
**LOGOS:** "They circled around the valley and climbed the mountain"
**PNEUMA:** "wound around the valley, climbed the mountain"

**Issue:** PNEUMA's "wound around" is vivid but slightly imprecise. LOGOS' "circled around" is accurate.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "Circled around the valley and climbed the mountain."

---

### Disagreement 14 — Verse 11: Judith's cry to the gatekeepers

**EMET:** "God — our God — is with us, still showing his power in Israel and his might against our enemies"
**LOGOS:** "God is with us — our God — still showing his power in Israel"
**PNEUMA:** "God — our God — is with us! He is still showing his power in Israel"

**Issue:** The rearrangement of "our God" as an appositive or interrupt. Greek ho theos ho theos hēmōn — "God, the God of ours." The doubling is emphatic. EMET captures the doubling best.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "God is with us — our God — still showing his power in Israel and his might against our enemies." The dash-set appositive preserves the emphatic doubling.

---

### Disagreement 15 — Verse 12: Response of the men

**EMET:** "they hurried down to the gate"
**LOGOS:** "they rushed down to the city gate"
**PNEUMA:** "they came running down to the gate"

**Issue:** "Hurried" vs. "rushed" vs. "came running." All render katadramontes (lit. "running down").
**SOPHIA ruling:** "They rushed down to the city gate" — "rushed" captures the urgency; "city gate" adds specificity.

---

### Disagreement 16 — Verse 14: Structure of the praise

**EMET:** "Praise God — praise him! Praise God, who has not withdrawn his mercy"
**LOGOS:** "Praise God — praise him! Praise God, who has not withdrawn his mercy"
**PNEUMA:** "Praise God — praise him! Praise God, who never withdrew his mercy"

**Issue:** "Has not withdrawn" (present perfect) vs. "never withdrew" (simple past). The Greek aorist ouk apestēsen.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "Has not withdrawn" — the present perfect captures the ongoing and completed nature of God's faithfulness better than simple past.

---

### Disagreement 17 — Verse 15: "supreme commander" vs. "commander"

**EMET:** "the commander of the Assyrian army"
**LOGOS:** "the supreme commander of the Assyrian army"
**PNEUMA:** "supreme commander of the Assyrian army"

**Issue:** Greek archēstrategon — "chief general/commander-in-chief." LOGOS/PNEUMA's "supreme commander" captures the compound.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "The supreme commander of the Assyrian army" — the compound deserves translation.

---

### Disagreement 18 — Verse 15: "while he lay drunk" vs. "beneath which he lay drunk"

**EMET:** "the canopy under which he lay in his drunkenness"
**LOGOS:** "the canopy beneath which he lay drunk"
**PNEUMA:** "the canopy he was lying under when he was drunk"

**Issue:** "In his drunkenness" is more formal and literal; "drunk" is simpler. The Greek en tē methē autou — "in his drunkenness."
**SOPHIA ruling:** "Beneath which he lay drunk" — concise and clear.

---

### Disagreement 19 — Verse 16: "my face that deceived him to his ruin"

**EMET:** "it was my face that deceived him to his destruction"
**LOGOS:** "it was my face that deceived him to his ruin"
**PNEUMA:** "it was my face that led him to his ruin"

**Issue:** "Deceived" vs. "led" — Greek ēpatēsen means deceived/beguiled. PNEUMA's "led" softens the deception element that is central.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "It was my face that deceived him to his ruin" — the deception is the point; "destruction" vs. "ruin" — LOGOS' "ruin" is more idiomatic.

---

### Disagreement 20 — Verse 16: Judith's purity declaration

**EMET:** "he did not commit sin with me to defile me and shame me"
**LOGOS:** "he committed no sin against me to defile and shame me"
**PNEUMA:** "He never touched me. He never defiled me. My honor is untouched."

**Issue:** PNEUMA unpacks the statement into three sentences — a legitimate rhetorical choice but diverges from the single clause in Greek. The Greek is one statement: ouk ēmartosin eis eme en deiasmō kai en aischynē.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "He committed no sin against me to defile and shame me" — the single clause preserved. PNEUMA's expansion, while emphatic, is interpretive addition.

---

### Disagreement 21 — Verse 18: Uzziah's blessing formula

**EMET:** "Blessed are you, daughter, above all women upon the earth"
**LOGOS:** "Blessed are you, daughter, above all women on the earth"
**PNEUMA:** "Blessed are you, daughter — blessed above all women on the face of the earth"

**Issue:** "Upon the earth" vs. "on the earth" vs. "on the face of the earth." Greek epi pasēs tēs gēs — "upon all the earth." Minor register variation; PNEUMA adds "face of."
**SOPHIA ruling:** "Blessed are you, daughter, above all women on the earth." Clean and resonant with the Jael blessing it echoes.

---

### Disagreement 22 — Verse 20: "brought low" vs. "humbled"

**EMET:** "when our people were brought low"
**LOGOS:** "when our nation was brought low"
**PNEUMA:** "when our people were brought low"

**Issue:** "People" vs. "nation" — Greek ethnos = "people/nation." Both valid. Minor.
**SOPHIA ruling:** "When our nation was brought low" — "nation" captures the political-covenantal community better here, given the military context.

---

## Summary

Total disagreements: 22
Most significant: v. 8 (THE central sentence), v. 2 ("drowned in wine"), v. 16 (declaration of purity), v. 15 ("supreme commander")
Unanimous agreements: vv. 4-5 (prayer address)
Typological echo flagged: v. 18 blessing formula = Judges 5:24 (Deborah's blessing of Jael)
Theological notes: v. 16 is the theological heart of the return scene — Judith's integrity and purity are God's gift to her, not merely a plot convenience.
